lines.text: In 1960, two men reached the deepest point on Earth.
Before the sand clouded the window, one of them saw something on the bottom.
They had no camera. Nobody believed him.
Sixty years later, a research team went back. With cameras this time.
On the first dive, the lights caught a pale shape at the edge of the dark.
It didn't swim away. It held still. Like it was watching.
On the second dive, it had a face.
Two holes for eyes. A slit for a mouth. Like a child's drawing of a person.
Every time the pilot moved, it moved the same way.
A second too late.
But the strangest part wasn't that it copied them.
It was that it was getting better at it.
Dive three: eyelids. Dive four: eyebrows, lips, teeth.
The marine biologist said it was a known species. She couldn't name it.
On dive five, it smiled at the camera.
The crew realized it wasn't copying faces in general.
It was copying theirs.
The pilot refused to go down again.
So the cameraman went alone.
The tape recovered from that dive is 41 minutes long.
For forty minutes, there's only dark water.
Then the cameraman turns the camera toward himself.
He's smiling.
It wasn't his face.
The sub came back up on its own. The cabin was empty.
The project was shut down. The footage was classified.
Piccard never went back down. Until he died, he never described what he saw.
Somewhere at the bottom, something has three faces now.
Maybe the question isn't what it is. Maybe it's whose face it wants next.
